title: Design of a Next-Generation Hand Mixer
text:
This project aimed to modernize an existing design by enhancing its appearance and implementing mechanical improvements for better functionality.



Comparison between Current Generation Smeg Hand Mixer and Next Generation Design




The benchmark design for this next generation model is the SMEG Hand Mixer HMF01. After examining the reviews placed by consumers, it was clear that many features were well-loved, but others still had room for improvement. Based on these reviews and personal experience, some changes that I decided to make for the Next-Generation of the SMEG Hand Mixer include:

An eject button for taking the beaters out instead of an eject switch, allowing for easier access and a smoother eject process.
An included charger case so the cord doesn’t get in the way during use, transitioning the mixer to be powered by a rechargeable battery.
An included bowl rest located near the bottom back of the mixer so that a user can set the mixer on the edge of the bowl when not in use.
A larger surface area on the ergonomic grip (a highly rated feature).
An included storage case (combined with charger case) so the user can easily keep track of attachments.
A styling update, including a flatter handle that doesn’t connect back into the body at the back.
Modernization, including an updated button / screen interface.







Parts of Completed Assembly







Key Features of Next-Gen Design





The next generation design also keeps recognizable and consumer approved features of the original design, namely:

The same approximate size
The smooth, retro look
The self-balancing design
The nine speed options and LED display with set timer











Ideation Sketches




After deciding what changes to make for the next generation design, I began sketching ideas to implement each design change. Once I had chosen a design, I moved into the 3D modeling phase.







I began by sketching the steps for each part of the mixer. Then, using the parametric modeling platform Onshape, I created my model.

Most parts in the assembly were created using a master model and offset surfaces.
The body of the master model was created with a revolve.
The handle was formed using a complex loft that follows a guide curve.






Final Design

















Thickness AnalysisInjection Molding Prep







Interference Check Mechanical Clearances







Zebra AnalysisCurvature Continuity





During the iterative modeling process, I conducted a series of computational validations to ensure manufacturing readiness:

Interference Testing: Verified that all internal gear meshes and housing tolerances were intentional, preventing mechanical clashing.
Thickness Analysis: Confirmed constant wall thickness across the chassis to facilitate high-quality injection molding.
Zebra Striping: Evaluated surface continuity to ensure light reflections flow smoothly across the curves of the mixer.










Engineering Drawings




The final step after hours of parametric modeling was to document my work. This includes the creation of engineering drawings and the complilation of a design package.

title: Statistical Analysis of Punxsutawney Phil’s Groundhog Day Predictions
text:
The aim of this project was to evaluate the accuracy of Punxsutawney Phil’s Groundhog Day predictions using historical weather data. Specifically, it investigates whether Phil’s shadow-based forecasts correlate with actual changes in average temperatures between February and March.




Photo by Camerauthor Photos on Unsplash

title: The Marmot’s Margin of Error: Quantifying the Groundhog’s Gaze
text:
Intro
Every year on February 2nd, thousands gather in Punxsutawney, Pennsylvania, awaiting the spring forecast from the world’s most famous groundhog, Punxsutawney Phil. According to tradition, if Phil sees his shadow, six more weeks of winter are expected. However, if he doesn’t see his shadow, an early spring is on the way.
While the event is a beloved cultural ritual, many question the accuracy of Phil’s predictions. Is there any truth behind the shadow-based forecasting, or is it simply superstition? To investigate, I analyzed historical average temperature data alongside Phil’s annual predictions to evaluate whether his forecasts align with actual weather patterns. Leaning toward belief rather than skepticism, I hypothesized that Punxsutawney Phil is correct more than half of the time.

title: Statistical Analysis of Punxsutawney Phil’s Groundhog Day Predictions
text:
Methods
To test this hypothesis, a one-sample hypothesis test for proportions was used. The null hypothesis was that Phil is correct less than or equal to 50% of the time. The alternative hypothesis was that he is correct more than 50% of the time. I set conditions for a “correct” prediction and analyzed the data under four different thresholds for defining winter (a difference of 0°C (no change), the mean of the distribution (7.88℉ increase), the median (7.96℉ increase), the 25th percentile (5.29℉ increase) ). Using if statements in Python, I determined whether each prediction was correct according to the defined threshold, and calculated the proportion of correct predictions for each method. For hypothesis testing and confidence intervals, I used norm.cdf or norm.ppf from the scipy.stats library.

title: Statistical Analysis of Punxsutawney Phil’s Groundhog Day Predictions
text:
Results
Results for the evaluation of the proportion of correct predictions for each definition of winter are shown in Figure 1.

After calculating the proportion of correct predictions, I used a one-sample hypothesis test for proportions, with hypotheses outlined in the methods section. The results are outlined in Table 1, along with the results for a 95% confidence interval for the true population proportion of accurate predictions. None of the p values for the proportion of predictions were statistically significant at a level of 𝛂 = 0.05.



Table 1: A summary of statistics obtained from a hypothesis test for proportions and a computed confidence interval for a population proportion of correct predictions made by Punxsutawney Phil.

title: Statistical Analysis of Punxsutawney Phil’s Groundhog Day Predictions
text:
Discussion
Because none of the p values are large, we have no basis for rejecting our null hypothesis. Therefore, we fail to reject the null hypothesis, and cannot conclude that Phil’s predictions are correct more than 50 percent of the time. It appears that Punxsutawney Phil’s predictions do not significantly outperform random chance under any of the thresholds tested. While the folklore is entertaining and charming, the data suggests that Phil may not be a reliable source of meteorological insight. Similarly, the calculated confidence intervals provide a region in which we can be 95% confident that the true population proportion of correct predictions lies.

title: Calculation Experimental Drag and Friction Coefficients from Coasting Car Data
text:
When a car moves without engine power, it gradually slows due to environmental forces like gravity, friction, and air resistance. By examining this natural deceleration, we can learn how these forces affect vehicle motion. In this project, data from a 2016 Aston Martin DB9 coasting on a gentle incline was analyzed to estimate friction and drag effects. The results provide insight into how external forces influence vehicle performance during real-world motion.




Photo by Roberto Nickson on Unsplash

title: Calculation Experimental Drag and Friction Coefficients from Coasting Car Data
text:
When a car moves without engine power, it gradually slows due to environmental forces like gravity, friction, and air resistance. By examining this natural deceleration, we can learn how these forces affect vehicle motion. In this project, data from a 2016 Aston Martin DB9 coasting on a gentle incline was analyzed to estimate friction and drag effects. The results provide insight into how external forces influence vehicle performance during real-world motion.




Photo by Roberto Nickson on Unsplash

title: Calculation Experimental Drag and Friction Coefficients from Coasting Car Data
text:
The Process
To analyze the motion of a car coasting both uphill and downhill on an inclined plane, we began by constructing free-body diagrams for each scenario. These diagrams account for the force of gravity, the normal force, aerodynamic drag (\(F_d\)), and rolling friction (\(F_r\)). Using the free-body and corresponding kinetic diagrams, we derived the equations of motion by applying Newton’s second law in the direction of motion.

After deriving the necessary equations, we followed these steps:

Numerical Integration: Converted the second-order equations into a system of first-order ordinary differential equations (ODEs), solved using Python’s scipy.integrate.odeint.
Parameter Optimization: Performed a manual iterative fit of the drag coefficient \(C_d\) and the coefficient of kinetic friction \(k\) to align the simulated velocity curves with experimental “North” and “South” data sets.
Sensitivity Analysis: Conducted uncertainty quantification by introducing a \(\pm 5\%\) variation in final velocity (\(v_f\)) to establish confidence intervals for our fitted parameters.

title: Calculation Experimental Drag and Friction Coefficients from Coasting Car Data
text:
Results
The best-fit parameters that matched the experimental data were \(C_d = 0.3283\) and \(k = 0.0170\). Using these values, the modeled curves closely aligned with the measured data, as shown in the velocity-time comparison.

title: Calculation Experimental Drag and Friction Coefficients from Coasting Car Data
text:
Discussion
The coefficient of drag \(C_d\) primarily influences vehicle deceleration at higher speeds due to its quadratic relationship with velocity, making it more dominant during the early phase of coast-down. In contrast, the rolling friction coefficient \(k\) exerts a near-constant effect and is more significant at lower speeds.
Because of this, the effects of \(C_d\) and \(k\) can be distinguished by examining how quickly velocity drops early in the coast versus how it behaves near the end. However, there is still some flexibility—it is possible to slightly increase one parameter while decreasing the other and still achieve a visually similar fit. This limits the precision with which either parameter can be determined individually, a trade-off we quantified through our confidence interval analysis.

title: The Dynamics of Deceleration: Determining Friction Coefficients from Numerical Analysis
text:
Results
The best-fit parameters that matched the experimental data were \(C_d = 0.3283\) and \(k = 0.0170\). Using these values, the modeled curves closely aligned with the measured data, as shown in the velocity-time comparison.

title: The Dynamics of Deceleration: Determining Friction Coefficients from Numerical Analysis
text:
Discussion
The coefficient of drag \(C_d\) primarily influences vehicle deceleration at higher speeds due to its quadratic relationship with velocity, making it more dominant during the early phase of coast-down. In contrast, the rolling friction coefficient \(k\) exerts a near-constant effect and is more significant at lower speeds.
Because of this, the effects of \(C_d\) and \(k\) can be distinguished by examining how quickly velocity drops early in the coast versus how it behaves near the end. However, there is still some flexibility—it is possible to slightly increase one parameter while decreasing the other and still achieve a visually similar fit. This limits the precision with which either parameter can be determined individually, a trade-off we quantified through our confidence interval analysis.

In order to determine the initial stresses on the scissor jack pin, we first simplified the geometry of the pin slightly using SpaceClaim. Then, we followed these steps using the ANSYS software:

Applied relevant boundary conditions
Selected correct material properties (in this case, those of structural steel)
Created an effective mesh using the automatic mesh and manual refinement
Applied the mesh convergence tool to ensure our mesh was sufficient
Validated our model using simple hand calculation

The generated stress plot following these steps is shown in Figure 1.

To improve the part, we wanted to increase the safety factor, so we aimed to reduce the maximum bending stress experienced by the pin. Since stress is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area, we decided to increase the pin’s cross-sectional area to lower the bending stress. We focused on bending stress because it was identified as the largest contributing factor to potential failure.
Two critical regions were identified as likely to experience the highest bending moments: the center of the part, and the location near the fillet, where there is a change in cross section. To compare these regions, we analyzed the bending moments using calculations that can be found in the completed report. These calculations communicated that an increase of the smaller diameter of the pin to 0.785 inches would increase the safety factor of the part from 0.58 to 2. The stress from the design change is shown in Figure 2.

If we were to make additional design changes, we would focus on strengthening the pin, since it is the component that limits the allowable load. We could increase its diameter even more or use a higher-strength material to raise the safe operating load. We would also aim to reduce stress concentrations by adding larger fillets, which would help lower peak stresses in critical areas. These changes together would allow the jack to safely support higher loads while maintaining our factor of safety of 2.

Pin Design Recommendations
To determine the baseline stress distribution, we simplified the pin geometry using SpaceClaim and performed a static structural analysis within ANSYS. The simulation was executed through the following methodology:

Boundary Conditions: Applied fixed supports and load vectors to simulate real-world vehicle lifting.
Material Properties: Assigned structural steel properties to the geometry.

Validation: Utilized a mesh convergence tool and validated the results against closed-form hand calculations.

The resulting von Mises stress distribution is shown in Figure 1.

To improve the design, we sought to increase the Factor of Safety by reducing the maximum bending stress. Since bending stress is inversely proportional to the section modulus, we increased the pin’s cross-sectional area. We focused specifically on bending as it was identified as the primary failure mode.
Analysis revealed two critical regions prone to high bending moments: the center of the pin and the fillet transition near the change in cross-section. Calculations showed that increasing the smaller diameter of the pin to 0.785 inches would raise the factor of safety from 0.58 to 2.0. The updated stress profile is shown in Figure 2.

Further optimizations would include increasing the diameter further or selecting high-strength alloys to raise the allowable load. Additionally, implementing larger radii fillets would mitigate stress concentrations, allowing the jack to safely support higher loads while maintaining a consistent factor of safety greater than or equal to 2.

text:
Traffic engineers frequently employ fluid dynamics to model vehicular flow at a macroscopic scale. title: Model of Traffic Using Fluids Flow Equations
text:
Simulation Conditions
The goal was to be able to model two common traffic situations: a red light turning green and traffic approaching a lane closure.

Condition 1: Red light at x = 300 m for 250 frames



Video
Runtime Video





Condition 2: Bottom lane closed at x = 300 m



Video
Runtime Video

title: Model of Traffic Using Fluids Flow Equations
text:
Methods

The LWR Model
The Lighthill-Whitman-Richards (LWR) model is a 1D approximation of traffic flow that utilizes the conservation equation.

Reynolds Transport Theorem (RTT): The model begins by applying the Reynolds Transport Theorem to cars to solve in differential form \[\frac{dB_{sys}}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt} \int_{CV} \rho \, dV + \int_{CS} \rho (\vec{v} \cdot \vec{n}) \, dA\]
Conservation of Cars: By applying the conservation of cars, the equation simplifies to the fundamental traffic flow PDE \[\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial (\rho v)}{\partial x} = 0\]
Greenshields Closure: To relate velocity (\(v\)) and density (\(\rho\)), the Greenshields model is applied \[v(\rho) = v_{max} \left( 1 - \frac{\rho}{\rho_{max}} \right)\]



Numerical Implementation: Solving the LWR Model
To simulate the model, finite difference methods are used to solve the partial differential equations.

Lax-Friedrichs Finite Difference (Flux Form): This method is used to handle the forward flux of traffic \[\rho_j^{n+1} = \frac{1}{2}(\rho_{j+1}^n + \rho_{j-1}^n) - \frac{\Delta t}{2\Delta x}(f_{j+1}^n - f_{j-1}^n)\]
Fick’s Law: To account for lane merging or sideways movement, Fick’s Law is incorporated \[J = -D \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial x}\]
Fully Formed PDE: The final simulation uses a combined PDE featuring both the LWR forward flux and Fick’s Law sideways diffusion \[\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial f(\rho)}{\partial x} = D \frac{\partial^2 \rho}{\partial x^2}\]

title: Model of Traffic Using Fluids Flow Equations
text:
Discussion
The simulations confirm that our mathematical framework accurately replicates macroscopic traffic phenomena, specifically the formation of back-propagating shockwaves at red lights and rarefaction waves during green-light dissipation. In lane closures, the model successfully captures the bottleneck effect, with density accumulating at the obstruction and diffusing laterally into adjacent lanes.

title: Model of Traffic Using Fluids Flow Equations
text:
Model Limitations
Despite its strengths, the model’s predictive accuracy is constrained by two primary factors:

Absence of Human Latency: The model assumes instantaneous acceleration. In reality, “start-up lost time” (human reaction delay) means real-world queues clear much slower than the fluid continuum suggests.
Macroscopic Simplifications:

Homogeneity: It assumes all vehicles behave identically, ignoring the varied dynamics of trucks versus passenger cars.
Continuum Hypothesis: Treating traffic as a fluid reduces accuracy in low-density scenarios where individual driver behavior dominates.
Reduced Dimensionality: By modeling density purely as a function of space (x) and time (t), we overlook the impacts of road grade, curvature, and complex weaving.

title: Model of Traffic Using Fluids Flow Equations
text:
Conclusion
The alignment between the simulation and expected physical wave patterns validates the use of Reynolds Transport Theorem and Fick’s Law for broad flow analysis, even while acknowledging these inherent behavioral gaps.

"""
Created on Wed Mar 11 10:32:01 2026

@author: micha
"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation

#%%#-----------------------------------Define Road-----------------------------------#
'''Lets you set physical constants of the model, such as length of the road, number of nodes to split the length into,
how many lanes there are, and the number of time steps over which the simulation runs'''
L = 1000 #m
num_nodes = 400 #number of discrete nodes
num_lanes = 3 #number of lanes on the road
dx = L/num_nodes #size of each node, m

dt = 0.5*dx #time step
T = 250 #number of time steps

x = np.linspace(0,L,num_nodes,endpoint=False) #array of node positions
road_rho = np.zeros((num_lanes, num_nodes)) #blank array to represent density of cars at each node

#%%#---------------------------------Road Initial Conditions--------------------------------#

#-------------------Initial Conditions, set inital densities on the road--------------------#
'''Lets you set the inital density on the road, with 0 being empty and 1 being ubmper to bumper traffic'''
#lane 3
road_rho[2, x<=200] = 0.6
road_rho[2, (x > 200) & (x < 400)] = 0.0
road_rho[2, x>=400] = 0.0

#lane 2
road_rho[1, x<=200] = 0.8
road_rho[1, (x > 300) & (x < 500)] = 0.0
road_rho[1, x>=500] = 0.0

#lane 1
road_rho[0, x<=200] = 0.6
road_rho[0, (x > 200) & (x < 400)] = 0.0
road_rho[0, x>=400] = 0.0

#---------------------------------------Light placement-------------------------------------#
'''Lets you place a stoplight that is by default set to be red, and a time frame at which it will turn green'''
light_x = 300
light_idx = int(light_x/dx) #this is the index we will assume the light is at
green_frame = 150

#------------------------------------Lane closure-------------------------------------------#
'''Lets you set which lanes are closed, as well as what time frame they close and over what range they close'''
closed_lanes = [1, 2]
close_frame = 50
left_close_x = 300
right_close_x = 600
left_close_idx = int(left_close_x/dx)
right_close_idx = int(right_close_x/dx)

#------------------------------------Lane changing------------------------------------------#
'''Lets you how fast density diffusion happens across lanes, both normally and when a lane is closed'''
D = 0.005 #represents lane change strength in the diffusion term
D_closed = 0.05 #represents lane change strength for a closed lane

#%%#-----------------------------------Step Through Time------------------------------------#
def q(rho):
    '''Finds the flow rate of cars as a function of density. Density is a range of empty road = 0 to no space = 1'''
    u = 1-rho #u is a range from stopped = 0 to umax (the speed limit) = 1
    q = rho*u
    return q

def LF_flux(rho_left, rho_right):
    alpha = 1.0
    return 0.5 * (q(rho_left) + q(rho_right)) - 0.5 * alpha * (rho_right - rho_left)

def time_forward_light(rho, light_color):
    '''Takes an array (referred to as rho) of form [lanes,nodes] and updates then returns
       the entire array in the same form using the Lax-Friedrichs finite difference
       Blocks flow at the light idx'''
    rho_new = np.zeros_like(rho) #Create

    for lane in range(num_lanes): #For each lane
        for idx in range(1,num_nodes-1): #For each node
            flux_right = LF_flux(rho[lane, idx], rho[lane, idx+1])
            flux_left  = LF_flux(rho[lane, idx-1], rho[lane, idx])

            if light_color == 'red':
                #No flux goes into the light index
                if idx == light_idx - 1:
                    flux_right = 0.0
                if idx == light_idx:
                    flux_left = 0.0

            #This is the Lax-Friedrichs finite difference approximation, meaning it uses a central difference to make sure waves can go both directions
            rho_new[lane, idx] = rho[lane, idx] - (dt / dx) * (flux_right - flux_left)

        #Simple left and right boundary condition
        rho_new[lane, 0] = rho[lane, 0]
        rho_new[lane, -1] = rho[lane, -1]

    return rho_new

def time_forward_closure(rho, lane_status):
    '''Takes an array (referred to as rho) of form [lanes,nodes] and updates then returns
       the entire array in the same form using the Lax-Friedrichs finite difference
       Blocks flow between the left and right closed idx'''
    rho_new = np.zeros_like(rho) #Create copy to store new values

    for lane in range(num_lanes): #For each lane
        for idx in range(1,num_nodes-1): #For each node
            flux_right = LF_flux(rho[lane, idx], rho[lane, idx+1])
            flux_left  = LF_flux(rho[lane, idx-1], rho[lane, idx])

            if lane_status == 'closed' and lane in closed_lanes:
                #No flux goes into the closed section
                if idx == left_close_idx - 1:
                    flux_right = 0.0
                if left_close_idx < idx < right_close_idx:
                    flux_left = 0.0
                    flux_right = 0.0
                if idx == right_close_idx:
                    flux_left = 0.0

            #This is the Lax-Friedrichs finite difference approximation, meaning it uses a central difference to make sure waves can go both directions
            rho_new[lane, idx] = rho[lane, idx] - (dt / dx) * (flux_right - flux_left)

        #Simple left and right boundary condition
        rho_new[lane, 0] = rho[lane, 0]
        rho_new[lane, -1] = rho[lane, -1]

    return rho_new

def time_forward_lanechange(rho, lane_status):
    '''Takes an array (referred to as rho) of form [lanes,nodes] and updates then returns
       the entire array in the same form using a Fick's Law of Diffusion equation to move
       density between adjacent lanes'''

    rho_new = np.zeros_like(rho) #Create copy to store new values

    for lane in range(num_lanes): #For each lane
        for idx in range(1,num_nodes-1): #For each node

            #Set default diffusion coefficient values
            D_10 = D
            D_21 = D

            #Change D value to be higher in a closed lane
            if lane_status == 'closed':
                if 2 in closed_lanes:
                    D_21 = D_closed
                if 1 in closed_lanes:
                    D_10 = D_closed
                    D_21 = D_closed
                if 0 in closed_lanes:
                    D_10 = D_closed

            #Fick's flux between lane 0 and 1 (positive goes from 1 into 0)
            Fi_flux_10 = D_10 * (rho[1, idx] - rho[0, idx])

            #Fick's flux between lane 1 and 2 (positive goes from 2 into 1)
            Fi_flux_21 = D_21 * (rho[2, idx] - rho[1, idx])

            #If the index is in the closed region and the lane is closed
            if left_close_idx < idx < right_close_idx and lane_status == 'closed' and 2 in closed_lanes:
                if Fi_flux_21 < 0: #If the flux has cars moving into the closed lane
                    Fi_flux_21 = 0

            if left_close_idx < idx < right_close_idx and lane_status == 'closed' and 1 in closed_lanes:
                if Fi_flux_10 < 0: #If the flux has cars moving into the closed lane
                    Fi_flux_10 = 0
                if Fi_flux_21 > 0: #If the flux has cars moving into the closed lane
                    Fi_flux_21 = 0


            if left_close_idx < idx < right_close_idx and lane_status == 'closed' and 0 in closed_lanes:
                if Fi_flux_10 > 0: #If the flux has cars moving into the closed lane
                    Fi_flux_10 = 0

            #Update lanes
            if lane == 2:
                rho_new[lane, idx] = rho[lane,idx] - Fi_flux_21
            if lane == 1:
                rho_new[lane, idx] = rho[lane,idx] - Fi_flux_10 + Fi_flux_21
            if lane == 0:
                rho_new[lane, idx] = rho[lane,idx] + Fi_flux_10

        #Simple left and right boundary condition
        rho_new[lane, 0] = rho[lane, 0]
        rho_new[lane, -1] = rho[lane, -1]

    return rho_new



#%%#-----------------------------------Plot Initial State-----------------------------------#
# plt.figure()
# plt.imshow(road_rho, aspect='auto', origin="lower", cmap="Reds")
# plt.xlabel("Position along road")
# plt.yticks([0.5, 1.5, 2.5], ["Lane 1", "Lane 2", "Lane 3"])
# plt.title('Initial Condition')
# plt.show()

#%%#-----------------------------------Plot Final State-------------------------------------#
#Steps forward going through each time step and plots the final state
# for i in range(T):
#     road_rho_new = time_forward_light(road_rho, 'green')
#     road_rho = road_rho_new

# plt.figure()
# plt.imshow(road_rho_new, aspect='auto', origin="lower", cmap="Reds")
# plt.xlabel("Position along road")
# plt.yticks([0.5, 1.5, 2.5], ["Lane 1", "Lane 2", "Lane 3"])
# plt.title('Final Condition')
# plt.show()

#%%#-----------------------------------Animation Setup--------------------------------------#

fig, ax = plt.subplots()

#Set the image we'll update as the road density array, populated with the inital values
img = ax.imshow(road_rho, aspect='auto', origin="lower", cmap="Reds", extent=[0, L, 0, num_lanes], interpolation='nearest', vmin= 0, vmax = 1)
scale = fig.colorbar(img, ax=ax)
scale.set_label('Traffic Density (ρ)')

ax.set_xlabel("Position along road (m)")
ax.set_yticks([0.5, 1.5, 2.5])
ax.set_yticklabels(["Lane 1", "Lane 2", "Lane 3"])
ax.set_ylim([0,3])

title = ax.set_title("Traffic Density at Time Step 0")

def first_frame():
    '''Sets the animation to the initial road density before any updates happen'''
    img.set_data(road_rho)
    title.set_text("Traffic Density at Time Step 0")
    return [img, title]

def update_light(frame, road_rho):
    '''Advances the simulation by one time step and updates the image'''
    if frame < green_frame:
        road_rho[:] = time_forward_lanechange(road_rho, 'red')
        road_rho[:] = time_forward_light(road_rho, 'red')
        title.set_text(f"Traffic Density at Time Step {frame + 1} - Red Light")
    else:
        road_rho[:] = time_forward_lanechange(road_rho, 'green')
        road_rho[:] = time_forward_light(road_rho, 'green')
        title.set_text(f"Traffic Density at Time Step {frame + 1} - Green Light")
    img.set_data(road_rho)
    return [img, title]

def update_closure(frame, road_rho):
    '''Advances the simulation by one time step and updates the image'''
    if frame < close_frame:
        road_rho[:] = time_forward_lanechange(road_rho, 'open')
        road_rho[:] = time_forward_light(road_rho, 'open')
        title.set_text(f"Traffic Density at Time Step {frame + 1} - Open Lanes")
    else:
        road_rho[:] = time_forward_lanechange(road_rho, 'closed')
        road_rho[:] = time_forward_closure(road_rho, 'closed')
        title.set_text(f"Traffic Density at Time Step {frame + 1} - Lane Closure")
    img.set_data(road_rho)
    return [img, title]

def update_lanechange(frame, road_rho):
    '''Advances the simulation by one time step and updates the image'''
    road_rho[:] = time_forward_lanechange(road_rho)

    title.set_text(f"Traffic Density at Time Step {frame + 1} - Open Lanes")
    img.set_data(road_rho)
    return [img, title]

#%%#-----------------------------------CHOOSE SITUATION!!-----------------------------------#
'''You must choose an update situation from the ones created for the program to run. Options are:
    * update = update_closure , this runs a situation where lanes 1 and 3 are closed after 100 frames
    * update = update_light , this runs a situation where there is a red light at x=300 for 150 frames
    * update = update_lanechange , this has no forward movement, but still diffuses density between adjacent lanes'''

update = update_closure

ani = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=T, fargs=(road_rho,), init_func=first_frame, interval=100, blit=False, repeat=False)
plt.show()

title: Mini Mars Rover Autonomous Robot
text:
Tasks

Leave Lander and Line Follow: The rover begins by exiting the lander and locking onto a white guidance track. We achieved this using an underside QRD sensor array, which calculates relative position offset to dynamically adjust motor differential output for precise line tracking.

Sample Collection and Return: Using IR and ultrasonic sensors for proximity detection, the rover aligns with the collection station to receive a ping pong ball payload. It then transports the sample and deposits it into the correct bin based on color feedback, leveraging a custom ball capture and release mechanism.
 
Canyon Navigation: In unmapped sections without guidance lines, the rover transitions to wall-following logic to navigate to the exit. We integrated ultrasonic sensors to detect forward obstacles; when a wall is encountered, the rover evaluates boundary clearances and steers toward open space.
Data Transmission: Upon returning to the lander base, the rover locates an active IR beacon and aims a targeting laser at a designated target. A servo-mounted sensor sweeps 180 degrees to identify the peak IR signal intensity, allowing the chassis to align before activating the laser.

title: Jordan Patten Hardy
text:
Tasks

Leave Lander and Line Follow The rover begins by exiting the lander and following a white line along the course. This was achieved using a QRD sensor array, which detects the rover’s position relative to the line and continuously adjusts its trajectory for accurate tracking.

Sample Collection and Return The rover detects the sample collection station using an IR sensor and positions itself to receive a ping pong ball. It then transports the sample and deposits it into the correct return bin based on color. This system combines IR and ultrasonic sensors for detection, along with a custom-designed ball capture and release mechanism.
 
Canyon Navigation In a section without guiding lines and enclosed by walls, the rover must autonomously navigate to the exit. This was accomplished using ultrasonic sensors to detect obstacles. When a wall is detected ahead, the rover turns in the direction with more open space, enabling efficient navigation through the canyon.
Data Transmission After returning to the lander, the rover must locate an IR beacon and accurately aim a laser at a target. A servo-mounted sensor scans for the strongest IR signal, allowing the rover to align itself before activating the laser to hit the target reliably.
